lesson.title: Careers in cyber security
lesson.subtitle: The jobs, the rules, and your first steps

video.title: Careers in cyber security
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer who visits schools to talk about security (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, speaking to the student)

scenes.visual: Dr Farah, in a school hall, shows an old photo of herself at a desk with screens in a mobile money company; a mug of tea steams.
scenes.animation: The photo slides in; the screens flicker with graphs.
scenes.narration: My first security job was at a mobile money company. Every morning, our team asked one question: what tried to get in last night? I haven’t been bored since.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: careers in cyber security — the jobs, the rules, and your first steps.

scenes.visual: Icons of a bank, a phone mast, a hospital and a school, each with a small shield; a world map with people of many backgrounds at desks.
scenes.narration: Every bank, phone company, hospital, government and school needs defenders. Around the world, millions of security jobs are waiting for people to fill them. And teams need people of every background: girls and boys, from every country.

scenes.visual: Three people at work: an analyst with alerts on a screen, an engineer drawing a sign-in system, an ethical hacker holding a signed permission letter.
scenes.animation: Each person appears as they are named.
scenes.narration: Here are some of the jobs. Security analysts watch the alarms and check the messages people report. Security engineers build defences, like the sign-in systems you use. And ethical hackers test systems to find weak spots before criminals do, but only with written permission.

scenes.visual: More people at work: an investigator with a magnifying glass over a laptop, a responder leading a team, a cryptographer at a board of numbers, a privacy officer with a folder, a trainer in front of a class.
scenes.animation: Each person slides in as they are named.
scenes.narration: There’s more. Forensic investigators work out what happened after an attack, and incident responders lead the clean-up. Cryptographers design the maths behind locks and keys. Privacy officers make sure people’s data is treated fairly, and trainers teach everyone to spot tricks.

scenes.visual: Clean card: a permission letter with a signature, a fence with a gate, and a stop line at the end of the fence.
scenes.animation: The signature writes itself; the stop line draws.
scenes.narration: One rule matters above all. Getting into a system without permission is a crime in almost every country, even “just to look”. Real defenders get written permission first, and stop exactly where it ends.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a sticky note with the office computer’s password, found on a desk; a student points towards the office door. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Mr Joseph slides in; cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A friend finds the office computer’s password on a sticky note and wants to “just look” around it. What do you do?

scenes.visual: The “say no and tell a teacher” card gets the check badge. The sticky note goes to a teacher, who changes the password.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the note changes hands.
scenes.narration: Say no, and tell a teacher where the password was. Looking without permission already breaks the law. Telling someone who can fix it is exactly what a defender does.

scenes.visual: A student’s backpack opens: a magnifying glass, a puzzle piece, a heart badge, a notebook and pen.
scenes.animation: Items hop out one by one.
scenes.narration: You don’t need to be a genius. You need curiosity, patience with puzzles, and honesty. Maths, computing and languages all help, and so does explaining things clearly, because defenders often explain problems to people who aren’t experts.

scenes.visual: A school computing club: students around one laptop solve a puzzle and capture a little flag; a free online course on a phone.
scenes.animation: A flag pops up on the screen; students cheer.
scenes.narration: You can start now. Join or start a computing club. Try capture-the-flag competitions made for students, where you solve security puzzles legally. And take free online courses, practising only on labs built for practice.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds up a phone showing a results page with someone else’s name on it. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. While checking your own results, you see another student’s details on the school website by mistake. What’s the ethical next step?

scenes.visual: The “tell the school privately” card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.on_screen_text: Needed everywhere · Many jobs · Permission first
scenes.narration: Tell the school privately, and go no further: don’t test more, and don’t share it. Remember: defenders are needed everywhere, there are many kinds of jobs, and permission comes first, always.

scenes.visual: A student trains a message filter on a laptop, then tells a friend about a security job over lunch.
scenes.animation: Messages sort into two piles; the friend leans in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: in the lab, train a phishing filter with examples, then test it with a tricky message it gets wrong. Then pick one security job, find out what a day in it looks like, and tell a friend.

checkpoints.prompt: A friend finds the office computer’s password on a sticky note and wants to “just look” around it. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, and tell a teacher where the password was

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — looking without permission is already a crime. Telling a teacher gets the password changed.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — getting in without permission is a crime even if nothing changes, and it’s no better if your friend does it alone. Say no, and tell a teacher.

checkpoints.prompt: While checking your own results, you see another student’s details on the school website by mistake. What’s the ethical next step?

options.text: Look around to see what else shows up
Tell the school privately, and go no further
Post a warning on social media

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — report it privately to the people who can fix it, and don’t test further or share it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — looking further is going where you have no permission, and posting it puts other students at risk. Tell the school privately and stop there.
